title: How to judge a supplement
goal: Explain how to judge a supplement: what it is for, how good the evidence is, why food comes first, the doping risk from contamination, and whether a small effect is worth it.

steps.title: What a supplement is for
steps.text:
A [dietary supplement](g:dietary-supplement) is anything taken on top of normal food: pills, powders, drinks, gels. The IOC sorts them by job [[c:fw-jobs]]:

| job | example |
|---|---|
| fix a shortfall | iron after a blood test shows low stores |
| convenient energy or protein | a gel during a race |
| direct performance gain | caffeine before a time trial |
| indirect gain (train, recover, stay healthy) | vitamin D in winter |

Only the third kind is an [ergogenic aid](g:ergogenic-aid) in the strict sense. Keep the scale in mind: for elite athletes, nutrition as a whole makes a small but valuable contribution, and supplements only a minor part of that [[c:fw-small]].

claims.text: Supplements target deficiencies, convenient energy and macronutrients, direct performance benefits, or indirect benefits such as supporting training.

evidence.quote: Products described as supplements target different issues, including (1) the management of micronutrient deficiencies, (2) supply of convenient forms of energy and macronutrients, and (3) provision of direct benefits to performance or (4) indirect benefits such as supporting intense training regimens.

claims.text: Nutrition makes a small contribution to elite performance; supplements a minor part of it.

evidence.quote: Nutrition usually makes a small but potentially valuable contribution to successful performance in elite athletes, and dietary supplements can make a minor contribution to this nutrition programme.

steps.title: Few products have good evidence
steps.text:
Shops are full of products that promise more speed. The IOC panel found good evidence of a performance benefit for only a few: [caffeine](g:caffeine), creatine, specific buffers and [dietary nitrate](g:dietary-nitrate) [[c:fw-few]].

Why so few? Most claims rest on the weakest kinds of evidence: athletes' stories, and a [mechanism](g:mechanistic-study) that explains how a product *might* help, with little or no test of whether it does [[c:fw-rigour]]. A mechanism shows something is possible; only a trial shows it works.

The gold standard is a [randomised](g:rct), [placebo](g:placebo)-controlled trial, ideally double-[blind](g:blinding), or a [crossover](g:crossover-study) in which each athlete gets both in random order [[c:fw-gold]].

claims.text: Only a few performance supplements (caffeine, creatine, specific buffers and nitrate) have good evidence of benefit.

evidence.quote: Supplements claiming to directly or indirectly enhance performance are typically the largest group of products marketed to athletes, but only a few (including caffeine, creatine, specific buffering agents and nitrate) have good evidence of benefits.

claims.text: Most information on supplement efficacy comes from anecdotes and mechanistic hypotheses with little evidence.

evidence.quote: However, most of the information around supplement efficacy in sport comes from models with the lowest rigour: anecdotes/observations from athletes; and scientific or mechanistic hypotheses that explain how a supplement might target a critical/limiting factor in performance, but with little to no evidence.

claims.text: The gold standard is a randomised, placebo-controlled (ideally double-blind) or counterbalanced crossover trial.

evidence.quote: The ‘gold standard’ for investigating the effects of supplements on sports performance is the prospective, randomised, controlled scientific trial, in which subjects are randomly allocated to receive either an experimental or placebo treatment (ideally in a double-blind manner) or crossed over to receive both treatments in counterbalanced order, under standardised conditions.

steps.title: Food first, then test in training
steps.text:
The IOC's order of steps is [food first](g:food-first). Before any supplement, a full look at what the athlete eats [[c:fw-assess]]. A performance supplement comes in only when strong evidence shows it is safe, legal and effective, and ideally once the everyday diet is right [[c:fw-only-when]].

Then: never try something new on race day. Try it in training or a simulated race first, at the dose and timing you plan to use [[c:fw-trial]]. Responses vary between people, and side effects such as gut trouble show up only when you try.

claims.text: A complete nutritional assessment should come before decisions about supplement use.

evidence.quote: A complete nutritional assessment should be undertaken before decisions regarding supplement use are made.

claims.text: Performance supplements should be considered only with a strong evidence base for safety, legality and effect, ideally after the diet is adequate.

evidence.quote: Performance-enhancing supplements should be considered only where a strong evidence base supports their use as safe, legal and effective, and ideally after adequacy of sports nutrition dietary practices is ensured.

claims.text: Performance supplements should be trialled in training or simulated competition before competition use.

evidence.quote: Supplements intended to enhance performance should be thoroughly trialled in training or simulated competition before being used in competition.

steps.title: The doping risk inside the bottle
steps.text:
A supplement can contain what its label doesn't say. In a study of 634 supplements bought in 13 countries, none sold as hormones, 94 (14.8%) held anabolic steroids that weren't on the label [[c:fw-geyer]]. Samples like this aren't random, so the true rate is unknown, and banned stimulants and other drugs have been found since [[c:fw-range]].

This [supplement contamination](g:supplement-contamination) can cause an [anti-doping rule violation](g:anti-doping-rule-violation) (ADRV) for an athlete who never meant to cheat. Even plain vitamin C and multivitamins have, rarely, been contaminated.

[Third-party testing](g:third-party-testing) of batches lowers the risk; nothing removes it [[c:fw-thirdparty]].

claims.text: Of 634 non-hormonal supplements from 13 countries, 14.8% contained anabolic steroids not declared on the label.

evidence.quote: From October 2000 until November 2001, 634 non-hormonal nutritional supplements were purchased in 13 countries from 215 different suppliers.
Out of the 634 samples analysed 94 (14.8 %) contained anabolic androgenic steroids not declared on the label ("positive supplements").

claims.text: The true prevalence of contamination is unknown; undeclared prohibited substances now span many classes and have rarely been found even in vitamin C and multivitamins.

evidence.quote: It is difficult to gain a perspective of the true prevalence of supplement contamination.
Nevertheless, it should also be recognised that common supplements, including vitamin C, multivitamins and minerals, have also been found, although rarely, to contain prohibited substances.

claims.text: Third-party testing schemes help manage contamination risk but cannot guarantee a product is safe.

evidence.quote: There can be no absolute guarantee that any product is entirely safe, but these schemes do help the athlete to manage the risk.

steps.title: Small effects, noisy tests
steps.text:
Supplements that work usually give gains of a few percent or less. For a top athlete that can matter: the [smallest worthwhile change](g:smallest-worthwhile-change) is often well under 1%.

But small effects are hard to see. Your own test-to-test noise (the [typical error](g:typical-error)) is often 1–2%, bigger than the effect, so one try with and one without can't tell you whether it worked. Studies need many athletes too: to pin down such gains, a crossover needs about 16–65 athletes [[c:fw-sample]]. Many supplement trials are far smaller.

So weigh both sides: a possible small gain against cost, the chance it does nothing, health risks and an ADRV [[c:fw-costs]].

claims.text: A crossover study measuring event performance needs about 16–65 athletes to pin down performance enhancements of the size that matter.

evidence.quote: Using change in performance in events as the outcome measure in a crossover study, researchers could delimit such enhancements with a sample of 16-65 athletes, or with 65-260 in a fully controlled study.

claims.text: Supplement decisions weigh rewards against costs: an ineffective product, health risks and an anti-doping rule violation.

evidence.quote: On the other side lie the costs, the possibility of using an ineffective supplement, the possible risks to health and the potential for an ADRV.

steps.title: What is 1% worth in a race?
steps.problem: A product claims a 1% gain. What is that in a 40 km bike time trial ridden in 60 min?
steps: A 1% gain in time means finishing 1% sooner.
Big enough to change a result, and also smaller than the day-to-day swing of many riders' times, which is why one trial at home can't prove it.

points: Supplements do four jobs: fix a shortfall, give convenient energy, improve performance directly, or help indirectly. Only a few performance supplements have good evidence: caffeine, creatine, specific buffers and nitrate.
Most claims rest on stories and mechanisms; only a controlled, ideally double-blind, trial shows a product works.
Food first: assess the diet before any supplement, and try a performance supplement in training before racing with it.
Supplements can hold undeclared banned substances: 14.8% of 634 products in one survey. Third-party batch testing lowers the risk but can't remove it.
Real effects are small, often smaller than your test-to-test noise, so one trial at home can't show they worked. Weigh the gain against cost, health and doping risk.

variants.stem: A triathlete takes iron tablets after a blood test showed low iron stores. Which job does this supplement do?

options.text: Fixing a shortfall
options.why: Right: it corrects a measured deficiency.

options.text: A direct performance gain
options.why: It may help performance, but only because it fixes a shortfall; in someone with normal iron it isn't an ergogenic aid.

options.text: Convenient energy
options.why: Iron supplies no energy; that job is for gels, drinks and bars.

options.text: Indirect gain in recovery
options.why: Its job here is to correct the deficiency the test found.

variants.stem: A cyclist eats an energy gel in the second hour of a race. Which job does it do?

options.text: Convenient energy
options.why: Right: a gel is a handy form of carbohydrate.

options.text: A direct performance gain like caffeine
options.why: Gels supply fuel; that is the 'convenient energy' job, unless one also contains caffeine.

options.text: Fixing a shortfall
options.why: Nothing was measured as deficient; it is fuel for the race.

options.text: Indirect gain in health
options.why: It fuels the effort in progress, not health.

variants.stem: A 'mitochondria booster' for runners is sold with three kinds of support. Which is the strongest evidence that it improves performance?

options.text: One double-blind crossover: 12 runners, 5 km 1.5% faster
options.why: Right: a controlled trial tests the outcome itself, though one small study is still weak.

options.text: A mouse study showing more mitochondria
options.why: Animal mechanism work shows something is possible, not that runners get faster.

options.text: Testimonials from two Olympic runners
options.why: Athletes' stories are the lowest rigour: no control, no blinding.

options.text: A clear explanation of how it should work
options.why: A mechanism is a hypothesis; it needs a trial.

variants.stem: A product's website explains in detail how it 'should' raise fat burning. Why isn't that enough to buy it?

options.text: A mechanism shows it might work, not that it does
options.why: Right: most supplement claims stop at the hypothesis stage, with little or no test.

options.text: Fat burning never helps endurance
options.why: Fat use matters in long events; the problem is the missing test, not the target.

options.text: Mechanisms are always wrong
options.why: Many are right; they still need a trial to show a real effect.

options.text: Only drugs can change fat burning
options.why: Training and diet change it too; the issue is evidence for this product.

variants.stem: A runner feels flat in training and asks which supplement to start. What does the IOC say should come first?

options.text: A full look at what she eats
options.why: Right: a complete nutritional assessment comes before supplement decisions.

options.text: Caffeine, since it has the best evidence
options.why: Good evidence for caffeine doesn't make it the answer to feeling flat; find the cause first.

options.text: A multivitamin, just in case
options.why: 'Just in case' skips the assessment and adds cost and contamination risk.

options.text: Whatever her training partners use
options.why: Others' habits are anecdote, the weakest evidence.

variants.stem: Three days before a 70.3 triathlon, an athlete reads about a supplement she has never used. Best plan?

options.text: Skip it now; try it in training after the race
options.why: Right: performance supplements should be trialled in training or a simulated race first.

options.text: Take a half dose on race day to be safe
options.why: A half dose is still untested: side effects or no effect, you find out mid-race.

options.text: Take it if the evidence is strong
options.why: Even a well-proven supplement can upset an individual; try it first.

options.text: Take a double dose to be sure it works
options.why: More dose, more risk of side effects, still untested.

variants.stem: A cyclist who is drug-tested wants a protein powder. Which choice lowers the doping risk most?

options.text: A product whose batch was third-party tested
options.why: Right: batch testing lowers the risk, though it can't guarantee a clean product.

options.text: A product labelled 'natural'
options.why: 'Natural' says nothing about contamination; many athletes wrongly read it as safe.

options.text: A product whose label lists no banned substance
options.why: Contaminants are by definition not on the label.

options.text: A product from a well-known brand
options.why: Brand size isn't a test; contaminated products came from many suppliers.

variants.stem: A triathlete says: "I only take plain vitamin C, so a positive doping test is impossible." Best reply?

options.text: Unlikely, but plain vitamin C has rarely been contaminated
options.why: Right: common supplements, including vitamin C and multivitamins, have occasionally contained banned substances.

options.text: Right: only sports supplements are contaminated
options.why: Contamination has been found, rarely, in common supplements too.

options.text: Right: vitamins are regulated like medicines
options.why: Many athletes believe this; it is a known cause of inadvertent positives.

options.text: Wrong: vitamin C itself is a banned substance
options.why: Vitamin C isn't banned; the risk is an undeclared contaminant.

variants.stem: A supplement gives a 2% gain. How much time is that in a 5 km run that takes 25 min?

options.why: This takes 2% of 2,500, as if 25 min were 2,500 s: a minutes-to-seconds slip.
This takes 2% of 25 and reads the minutes as seconds.

options.text: 3 s
options.why: This takes 0.2%, not 2%.

variants.stem: An Ironman bike leg takes 5 h. How much time is a 0.5% gain?

options.why: This is 5%, not 0.5%: a decimal slip.
This takes 0.5% of 3,000 s (50 min), not of 5 h.
This takes 0.5% of 300, the hours read as minutes.

variants.stem: A study: 8 recreational male cyclists, beetroot juice or placebo, 10 km time trial 1.2% faster, p = 0.04. What most limits applying it to you, a well-trained female triathlete?

options.text: 8 recreational men: small, and unlike you
options.why: Right: too few to pin down small effects, and results generalise only to athletes like those studied.

options.text: p = 0.04 means the effect is certainly real
options.why: A p-value isn't certainty; with 8 riders the estimate is imprecise.

options.text: A 1.2% gain is too small to matter in any race
options.why: 1.2% can decide a race; the problem is how well this study can measure it, and for whom.

options.text: Crossover studies can't test supplements
options.why: Crossovers suit short-acting supplements like beetroot juice.
